## Introduction

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > Introduction] 1 Part 35 is intended to limit the use of oral expert evidence to that which is reasonably required. In addition, where possible, matters requiring expert evidence should be dealt with by only one expert. Experts and those instructing them are expected to have regard to the guidance contained in the Guidance for the Instruction of Experts in Civil Claims 2014 at www.judiciary.gov.uk (opens in a new tab) . (Further guidance on experts is contained in Annex C to the Practice Direction (Pre-Action Conduct)).

## Expert Evidence – General Requirements

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > Expert Evidence – General Requirements] 2.1 Expert evidence should be the independent product of the expert uninfluenced by the pressures of litigation.

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > Expert Evidence – General Requirements] 2.2 Experts should assist the court by providing objective, unbiased opinions on matters within their expertise, and should not assume the role of an advocate.

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > Expert Evidence – General Requirements] 2.3 Experts should consider all material facts, including those which might detract from their opinions.

## 2.4 Experts should make it clear –

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.4 Experts should make it clear –] (a) when a question or issue falls outside their expertise; and

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.4 Experts should make it clear –] (b) when they are not able to reach a definite opinion, for example because they have insufficient information.

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.4 Experts should make it clear –] 2.5 If, after producing a report, an expert’s view changes on any material matter, such change of view should be communicated to all the parties without delay, and when appropriate to the court.

## 2.6

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (1) In a soft tissue injury claim, where permission is given for a fixed cost medical report, the first report must be obtained from an accredited medical expert selected via the MedCo Portal (website at: www.medco.org.uk (opens in a new tab) ).

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (1A) In a claim for a whiplash injury, whether or not it is part of a claim for other injuries—

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (a) where in respect of the claim for a whiplash injury, permission is given for a fixed cost medical report, the first report must be obtained from an accredited medical expert selected via the MedCo Portal;

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (b) where the claimant lives outside England and Wales, but chooses to be examined for the purposes of a medical report in England or Wales, paragraph (a) applies;

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (c) where the claimant obtains a medical report in respect of a more serious injury suffered on the same occasion as the whiplash injury, where permission is given, the claimant may use that report instead of a fixed costs medical report under paragraph (a) provided that—

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (i) the report is from a doctor who is listed on the General Medical Council’s Specialist Register; and

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (ii) the report provides evidence of the whiplash injury; and

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (d) unless paragraph (b) applies, in any other case where the claimant lives outside England and Wales, the medical report in respect of the claim for the whiplash injury (or, if there is more than one report, the first report) must be from a person who is recognised by the country in which they practise as—

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (i) being a medical expert; and

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (ii) having the required qualifications for the purposes of diagnosis and prognosis of a whiplash injury.

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (2) The cost of obtaining a further report from an expert not listed in rule 35.4(3C)(a) to (d) or (3C)(b)(i) to (iv) is not subject to rule 45.62(2)(b ) , but the use of that expert and the cost must be justified.

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (3)

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] In this paragraph—

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (a) in respect of a soft tissue injury claim, ‘accredited medical expert’, ‘fixed cost medical report’, ‘MedCo’, and ‘soft tissue injury claim’ have the same meaning as in paragraph 1.1(A1), (10A), (12A) and (16A), respectively, of the Pre-Action Protocol for Low Value Personal Injury Claims in Road Traffic Accidents; and.

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 2.6] (b) in respect of a claim for a whiplash injury, ‘fixed cost medical report’, ‘accredited medical expert’, ‘MedCo, and ‘whiplash injury’ have the same meaning as in paragraph 1.2(1), (17), (19) and (38) of the Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims Below the Small Claims Limit in Road Traffic Accidents.

## Form and Content of an Expert’s Report

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > Form and Content of an Expert’s Report] 3.1 An expert’s report should be addressed to the court and not to the party from whom the expert has received instructions.

## 3.2 An expert’s report must:

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (1) give details of the expert’s qualifications;

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (2) give details of any literature or other material which has been relied on in making the report;

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (3) contain a statement setting out the substance of all facts and instructions which are material to the opinions expressed in the report or upon which those opinions are based;

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (4) make clear which of the facts stated in the report are within the expert’s own knowledge;

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (5) say who carried out any examination, measurement, test or experiment which the expert has used for the report, give the qualifications of that person, and say whether or not the test or experiment has been carried out under the expert’s supervision;

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (6) where there is a range of opinion on the matters dealt with in the report –

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (a) summarise the range of opinions; and

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (b) give reasons for the expert’s own opinion;

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (7) contain a summary of the conclusions reached;

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (8) if the expert is not able to give an opinion without qualification, state the qualification; and

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (9) contain a statement that the expert –

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (a) understands their duty to the court, and has complied with that duty; and

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.2 An expert’s report must:] (b) is aware of the requirements of Part 35, this practice direction and the Guidance for the Instruction of Experts in Civil Claims 2014.

## 3.3 An expert’s report must be verified by a statement of truth in the following form –

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.3 An expert’s report must be verified by a statement of truth in the following form –] I confirm that I have made clear which facts and matters referred to in this report are within my own knowledge and which are not. Those that are within my own knowledge I confirm to be true. The opinions I have expressed represent my true and complete professional opinions on the matters to which they refer.

[PRACTICE DIRECTION 35 – EXPERTS AND ASSESSORS > 3.3 An expert’s report must be verified by a statement of truth in the following form –] I understand that proceedings for contempt of court may be brought against anyone who makes, or causes to be made, a false statement in a document verified by a statement of truth without an honest belief in its truth.

# Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.)

## Information

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Information] 4 Under rule 35.9 the court may direct a party with access to information, which is not reasonably available to another party to serve on that other party a document, which records the information. The document served must include sufficient details of all the facts, tests, experiments and assumptions which underlie any part of the information to enable the party on whom it is served to make, or to obtain, a proper interpretation of the information and an assessment of its significance.

## Instructions

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Instructions] 5 Cross-examination of experts on the contents of their instructions will not be allowed unless the court permits it (or unless the party who gave the instructions consents). Before it gives permission the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to consider that the statement in the report of the substance of the instructions is inaccurate or incomplete. If the court is so satisfied, it will allow the cross-examination where it appears to be in the interests of justice.

## Questions to Experts

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Questions to Experts] 6.1 Where a party sends a written question or questions under rule 35.6 direct to an expert, a copy of the questions must, at the same time, be sent to the other party or parties.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Questions to Experts] 6.2 The party or parties instructing the expert must pay any fees charged by that expert for answering questions put under rule 35.6. This does not affect any decision of the court as to the party who is ultimately to bear the expert’s fees.

## Single joint expert

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] 7 When considering whether to give permission for the parties to rely on expert evidence and whether that evidence should be from a single joint expert the court will take into account all the circumstances in particular, whether:

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (a) it is proportionate to have separate experts for each party on a particular issue with reference to –

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (i) the amount in dispute;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (ii) the importance to the parties; and

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (iii) the complexity of the issue;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (b) the instruction of a single joint expert is likely to assist the parties and the court to resolve the issue more speedily and in a more cost-effective way than separately instructed experts;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (c) expert evidence is to be given on the issue of liability, causation or quantum;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (d) the expert evidence falls within a substantially established area of knowledge which is unlikely to be in dispute or there is likely to be a range of expert opinion;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (e) a party has already instructed an expert on the issue in question and whether or not that was done in compliance with any practice direction or relevant pre-action protocol;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (f) questions put in accordance with rule 35.6 are likely to remove the need for the other party to instruct an expert if one party has already instructed an expert;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (g) questions put to a single joint expert may not conclusively deal with all issues that may require testing prior to trial;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (h) a conference may be required with the legal representatives, experts and other witnesses which may make instruction of a single joint expert impractical; and

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Single joint expert] (i) a claim to privilege (GL) makes the instruction of any expert as a single joint expert inappropriate.

## Orders

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Orders] 8 Where an order requires an act to be done by an expert, or otherwise affects an expert, the party instructing that expert must serve a copy of the order on the expert. The claimant must serve the order on a single joint expert.

## Discussions between experts

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Discussions between experts] 9.1 Unless directed by the court discussions between experts are not mandatory. Parties must consider, with their experts, at an early stage, whether there is likely to be any useful purpose in holding an experts’ discussion and if so when.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Discussions between experts] 9.2 The purpose of discussions between experts is not for experts to settle cases but to agree and narrow issues and in particular to identify:

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Discussions between experts] (i) the extent of the agreement between them;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Discussions between experts] (ii) the points of and short reasons for any disagreement;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Discussions between experts] (iii) action, if any, which may be taken to resolve any outstanding points of disagreement; and

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Discussions between experts] (iv) any further material issues not raised and the extent to which these issues are agreed.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Discussions between experts] 9.3 Where the experts are to meet, the parties must discuss and if possible agree whether an agenda is necessary, and if so attempt to agree one that helps the experts to focus on the issues which need to be discussed. The agenda must not be in the form of leading questions or hostile in tone.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Discussions between experts] 9.4 Unless ordered by the court, or agreed by all parties, and the experts, neither the parties nor their legal representatives may attend experts discussions.

## 9.5 If the legal representatives do attend –

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > 9.5 If the legal representatives do attend –] (i) they should not normally intervene in the discussion, except to answer questions put to them by the experts or to advise on the law; and

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > 9.5 If the legal representatives do attend –] (ii) the experts may if they so wish hold part of their discussions in the absence of the legal representatives.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > 9.5 If the legal representatives do attend –] 9.6 A statement must be prepared by the experts dealing with paragraphs 9.2(i) – (iv) above. Individual copies of the statements must be signed by the experts at the conclusion of the discussion, or as soon thereafter as practicable, and in any event within 7 days. Copies of the statements must be provided to the parties no later than 14 days after signing.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > 9.5 If the legal representatives do attend –] 9.7 Experts must give their own opinions to assist the court and do not require the authority of the parties to sign a joint statement.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > 9.5 If the legal representatives do attend –] 9.8 If an expert significantly alters an opinion, the joint statement must include a note or addendum by that expert explaining the change of opinion.

## Assessors

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Assessors] 10.1 An assessor may be appointed to assist the court under rule 35.15. Not less than 21 days before making any such appointment, the court will notify each party in writing of the name of the proposed assessor, of the matter in respect of which the assistance of the assessor will be sought and of the qualifications of the assessor to give that assistance.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Assessors] 10.2 Where any person has been proposed for appointment as an assessor, any party may object to that person either personally or in respect of that person’s qualification.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Assessors] 10.3 Any such objection must be made in writing and filed with the court within 7 days of receipt of the notification referred to in paragraph 10.1 and will be taken into account by the court in deciding whether or not to make the appointment.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Assessors] 10.4 Copies of any report prepared by the assessor will be sent to each of the parties but the assessor will not give oral evidence or be open to cross-examination or questioning.

## Concurrent expert evidence

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] 11.1 At any stage in the proceedings the court may direct that some or all of the evidence of experts from like disciplines shall be given concurrently. The procedure set out in paragraph 11.4 shall apply in respect of any part of the evidence which is to be given concurrently.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] 11.2 To the extent that the expert evidence is not to be given concurrently, the court may direct the evidence to be given in any appropriate manner. This may include a direction for the experts from like disciplines to give their evidence and be cross-examined on an issue-by-issue basis, so that each party calls its expert or experts to give evidence in relation to a particular issue, followed by the other parties calling their expert or experts to give evidence in relation to that issue (and so on for each of the expert issues which are to be addressed in this manner).

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] 11.3 The court may set an agenda for the taking of expert evidence concurrently or on an issue-by-issue basis, or may direct that the parties agree such an agenda subject to the approval of the court. In either case, the agenda should be based upon the areas of disagreement identified in the experts’ joint statements made pursuant to rule 35.12.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] 11.4 Where expert evidence is to be given concurrently, then (after the relevant experts have each taken the oath or affirmed) in relation to each issue on the agenda, and subject to the judge’s discretion to modify the procedure—

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] (1) the judge will initiate the discussion by asking the experts, in turn, for their views in relation to the issues on the agenda. Once an expert has expressed a view the judge may ask questions about it. At one or more appropriate stages when questioning a particular expert, the judge may invite the other expert to comment or to ask that expert’s own questions of the first expert;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] (2) after the process set out in (1) has been completed for any issue (or all issues), the judge will invite the parties’ representatives to ask questions of the experts. Such questioning should be directed towards:

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] (a) testing the correctness of an expert’s view;

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] (b) seeking clarification of an expert’s view; or

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] (c) eliciting evidence on any issue (or on any aspect of an issue) which has been omitted from consideration during the process set out in (1); and

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] (3) after the process set out in (2) has been completed in relation to any issue (or all issues), the judge may summarise the experts’ different positions on the issue and ask them to confirm or correct that summary.

[Part 22 deals with statements of truth. Rule 32.14 sets out the consequences of verifying a document containing a false statement without an honest belief in its truth.) > Concurrent expert evidence] Updated: Sunday, 1 October 2023
